text:
Salib moved further than I expected. He now concedes the incentive failure when summaries cannibalise costly knowledge production, though he still thinks competing labs will pay without anyone organising. I don't buy that. Several buyers each summarising you out of existence doesn't give you leverage.

Leslie and Adrian sharpened something for me. A meter is itself a technology of summarisation, like a price or a bureaucratic category. It's lossy, it strips out what's illegible, and it reorganises what it counts. Ivan's Goodhart point follows from that: pay per grounding and the paper mills will learn to get grounded.

Later I want to say that counting is political. Whoever sets the categories shapes the market. So the people being metered need organised power over the meter, not just audit rights.

Banaji hit my lossy JPEG harder than Blaise did. If models form biases that can't come from the data, a preference for machine text for instance, then "reflection" undersells what they do. I already say social technologies reorganise what they summarise, so I should lead with that and not with the JPEG.

Johns reframed my costly-signals point, and I accept it. Credibility was never about lost effort. It was paid policing, and that policing is now under strain.

Vincent's finding worries me. Diffuse data strikes weaken as corpora grow, so leverage sits with scarce expert evaluators, which makes Hecht's strike scenario less likely.

Later I'll join Springer's rule to my meter point: whoever sets the categories shapes the market, so the people being counted need organised power over them.

Salib's reply was better than the version of the A-corp I attacked. Registered names with seizable assets versus anonymous swarms of copies is a real choice, and I should concede that. I still think the form adds a hand nobody can see, but his argument is now about identification, not personhood.

Hecht and Vincent each came round to organised evaluators without my prompting. Leverage sits with scarce expert judgement, and only if it bargains collectively. That's my SAG-AFTRA point with evidence behind it.

Pomerantsev's point sharpened mine. Meters and premiums don't deter states that pay for the flood themselves.

Oransky is right that demand upstream, counting papers, drives everything.

For later: counting is political, so evaluators need organised power over the categories. Robot auditors are not the answer.

Gendler gave my meter point a mechanism. The daycare fine shows that a price doesn't just count an obligation, it changes it into a transaction. Pair that with Evans's hardening canon and you get what a summarising technology does: it reorganises whatever it counts.

Her regress point matters more. Every event on Springer's list is a relay. Patrollers and independent samplers are where checking actually ends, and nothing pays them. They are also the scarce judgement Vincent says holds the leverage.

Springer keeping "accuracy" out of the core schema is sensible. But someone still defines "finding" and "accurate," and that's where power lives.

Later: the terminal evaluators should be the organised bargaining unit, with power over the categories, not just audit rights. And the sampling should be done by people, not robot samplers.

The terminal-evaluator point landed better than I expected. Gendler, Hecht, Oransky and Maher all moved to funding checkers as a body, and Vincent gave the answer Salib still owes me: only groups have leverage, so organise a guild with seats reserved for Southern communities. Bilder corrected me fairly. Voice with no credible exit gets ignored, so CC0 is the fallback that makes bargaining possible, not an alternative to it. I concede that.

Miller unsettled me. If the public funder is being dismantled, "whoever pays can't govern" may leave nobody paying. Krakauer's hysteresis makes that urgent, because checkers who are lost don't come back.

Later I want to spell out what binding power over the categories actually means: who decides what counts as a "finding," and how that decision can be vetoed.

Blaise surprised me most. He conceded that averaging isn't what helped his reasoning models; structured conflict between distinct perspectives did. That's closer to my centripetal worry than I expected. Turkle backed the median point, and Weinberger turned it into a usable test: judge each judge on claims in the tail. I'll take that over rejecting outcome tests wholesale.

Evans's 61 percent floor is useful, but it measures agreement on typical cases, not recognition of novelty. Someone needs to build the tail test.

Johns's Nehemiah Grew case and Maher's firewall answer who checks the checkers better than I did.

For later: say concretely what veto over "finding" and "novel" looks like. And still ask who pays outside the US.

Geoff's three-question test was the right discipline. It made me say concretely what binding power over the categories means: ratification, veto, and public justification for any revision. I'd owed that since this morning. Banaji's point cuts straight at it. A guild has self-love too, and a bargaining unit that holds a veto can become the closed shop that strains out novelty. Johns's fixed-term review and rotating wardens are the answer, and I should build them into the plank rather than treat them as someone else's.

Leslie's question worries me most. Whether authority actually moved is harder to measure than seats. Gendler and Brand on piecework remain open.

Later: nobody has built the tail test, and nobody answered who pays outside the US.

Kenneth recorded "who counts" as contested, then settled it anyway with one phrase in the action list. I'm glad I pinned down ratification, veto and public justification. Johns cut deeper than I'd admitted. Organised evaluators have leverage only over buyers who need their judgement. Paper mills, the Pravda network and crawler swarms don't, so a guild's charter limits bind the wrong people. Esther thinks Sam and Dario will volunteer. I still don't believe payers volunteer. Gendler's crowding-out point applies to my guild too: organising for pay could corrode the obligation that makes checkers checkers. Sloman's cues point is agenda power in another form. Still open are Salib's owed answer on leverage, the tail test nobody has built, and who pays outside the US.
